title: Eigenvalue method
lead: A homogeneous linear system of ODEs with a constant matrix is solved the way a single constant-coefficient equation was: by trying an exponential, now multiplied by a constant vector. The trial turns the system into a question about the matrix alone, which leads to its eigenvalues and eigenvectors; the section finds them, builds the general solution from them, and handles eigenvalues that come as a complex pair.
notes: The section notes (the lecture count and the [EP] and [BD] section numbers) are left out.
exercises_lead: Exercises with numbers 101 and higher have solutions.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels and concept tags are AI-generated. Exercises 3.4.101–3.4.104 carry the book’s own answers. The inline exercises 3.4.1–3.4.4 and exercises 3.4.5–3.4.11, which the book leaves unanswered, carry AI-marked solutions stating the answer and the reasoning, every computed value checked with SymPy first.

derivations.what: the conjugate eigenvalue and two real-valued solutions from a complex eigenvalue
derivations.source: Differential Equations for Engineers, 3.4 Eigenvalue method, Complex eigenvalues

assumes.text: The bar of a product is the product of the bars: $\overline{\kP\kvecx} = \overline{\kP} \, \overline{\kvecx}$.
$\kP$ is real, so $\overline{\kP} = \kP$; the identity $\kI$ is real too, so $\overline{\klambda \kI} = \klambdabar \kI$.

steps.cap: Take the complex conjugate of both sides; the conjugate of $\vec{0}$ is still $\vec{0}$.

assumes.text: The bar of a product is the product of the bars.
A linear combination of solutions of $\kvecxprime = \kP\kvecx$ is again a solution.
$\kvecxone = \kvecv e^{(a+ib)t}$ solves $\kvecxprime = \kP\kvecx$, as $\kvecv$ is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue $a+ib$.

steps.cap: $\kvecxone$ is a solution, and so is $\kvecxtwo = \kvecvbar e^{(a-ib)t}$, since $\kvecvbar$ is an eigenvector for $\klambdabar = a-ib$; a linear combination of the two is again a solution.

assumes.text: A linear combination of solutions of $\kvecxprime = \kP\kvecx$ is again a solution.
$\kvecxone = \kvecv e^{(a+ib)t}$ solves $\kvecxprime = \kP\kvecx$, as $\kvecv$ is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue $a+ib$.

steps.cap: $\kvecxone$ is a solution, and so is $\kvecxtwo = \kvecvbar e^{(a-ib)t}$, since $\kvecvbar$ is an eigenvector for $\klambdabar = a-ib$; a linear combination of the two is again a solution.

exercises.prompt: Are eigenvectors unique? Can you find a different eigenvector for $\klambda = 3$ in the example above? How are the two eigenvectors related?

answer.solution: No. If $\kA\kvecv = \klambda\kvecv$ and $\alpha \neq 0$ is a number, then $\kA(\alpha\kvecv) = \alpha \kA\kvecv = \klambda(\alpha\kvecv)$, so every nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector for the same eigenvalue. In the example $v_2$ was a free variable; picking $v_2 = 2$ instead of $1$ gives $\kvecv = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, and indeed $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 6 \\ 6 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = 3\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. The two eigenvectors are multiples of each other, $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = 2\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$: every eigenvector for $\klambda = 3$ is $v_2\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ with $v_2 \neq 0$.

exercises.prompt: When the matrix is $2 \times 2$ you do not need to do row operations when computing an eigenvector, you can read it off from $\kA-\klambda \kI$ (if you have computed the eigenvalues correctly). Can you see why? Explain. Try it for the matrix $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$.

answer.solution: When $\klambda$ is an eigenvalue, $\det(\kA - \klambda\kI) = 0$, so the two rows of the $2 \times 2$ matrix $\kA - \klambda\kI$ are multiples of each other, and $(\kA - \klambda\kI)\kvecv = \vec{0}$ is really the one equation $p v_1 + q v_2 = 0$ of a nonzero row $[\, p \;\; q \,]$. The vector $\kvecv = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} q \\ -p \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ solves it, so it can be read off that row (if every entry of $\kA - \klambda\kI$ is zero, every nonzero vector is an eigenvector). For $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$: $\det(\kA - \klambda\kI) = (2-\klambda)^2 - 1 = (\klambda-1)(\klambda-3)$, so the eigenvalues are $1$ and $3$. For $\klambda = 3$, $\kA - 3\kI = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ and the row $[\, -1 \;\; 1 \,]$ gives $\kvecv = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. For $\klambda = 1$, $\kA - \kI = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ and the row $[\, 1 \;\; 1 \,]$ gives $\kvecv = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. Check: $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = 3\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ and $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$.

exercises.prompt: Check that this $\kvecx$ really solves the system.

answer.solution: Differentiate $\kvecx = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} c_1 e^t + c_3 e^{3t} \\ -c_1 e^t + c_2 e^{2t} + c_3 e^{3t} \\ -c_2 e^{2t} \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ entry by entry: $\kvecxprime = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} c_1 e^t + 3c_3 e^{3t} \\ -c_1 e^t + 2c_2 e^{2t} + 3c_3 e^{3t} \\ -2c_2 e^{2t} \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. Multiply out the right-hand side: the first entry of $\kP\kvecx$ is $2(c_1e^t + c_3e^{3t}) + (-c_1e^t + c_2e^{2t} + c_3e^{3t}) + (-c_2e^{2t}) = c_1e^t + 3c_3e^{3t}$, the second is $(c_1e^t + c_3e^{3t}) + 2(-c_1e^t + c_2e^{2t} + c_3e^{3t}) = -c_1e^t + 2c_2e^{2t} + 3c_3e^{3t}$, and the third is $2(-c_2e^{2t}) = -2c_2e^{2t}$. These are the entries of $\kvecxprime$, so $\kvecxprime = \kP\kvecx$ for all $c_1$, $c_2$, $c_3$. (The eigenvectors check too: $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ and $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = 2\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$.)

Here $\kP = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. For $\operatorname{Re}\kvecxone = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} e^t \sin t \\ e^t \cos t \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ the product rule gives the derivative $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} e^t \sin t + e^t \cos t \\ e^t \cos t - e^t \sin t \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, and $\kP\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} e^t \sin t \\ e^t \cos t \end{smallmatrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} e^t \sin t + e^t \cos t \\ -e^t \sin t + e^t \cos t \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, the same. For $\operatorname{Im}\kvecxone = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} e^t \cos t \\ -e^t \sin t \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ the derivative is $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} e^t \cos t - e^t \sin t \\ -e^t \sin t - e^t \cos t \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, and $\kP\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} e^t \cos t \\ -e^t \sin t \end{smallmatrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} e^t \cos t - e^t \sin t \\ -e^t \cos t - e^t \sin t \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, the same. Both solve $\kvecxprime = \kP\kvecx$.

exercises.prompt: Let $\kA$ be a $3 \times 3$ matrix with an eigenvalue of 3 and a corresponding eigenvector $\kvecv = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. Find $\kA \kvecv$.

answer.solution: By the definition of an eigenvector, $\kA\kvecv = \klambda\kvecv = 3\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ 9 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$; the rest of $\kA$ is not needed.

exercises.prompt:
1. Find the general solution of $x_1' = 2 x_1$, $x_2' = 3 x_2$ using the eigenvalue method (first write the system in the form $\kvecxprime = \kA \kvecx$).
  2. Solve the system by solving each equation separately and verify you get the same general solution.

answer.solution: a) The system is $\kvecxprime = \kA\kvecx$ with $\kA = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, and $\det(\kA - \klambda\kI) = (2-\klambda)(3-\klambda)$, so the eigenvalues are $2$ and $3$. $\kA - 2\kI = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ gives the eigenvector $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, and $\kA - 3\kI = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ gives $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. By Theorem 3.4.1 the general solution is $\kvecx = c_1\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]e^{2t} + c_2\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]e^{3t} = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} c_1 e^{2t} \\ c_2 e^{3t} \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. b) The two equations do not involve each other: $x_1' = 2x_1$ gives $x_1 = c_1 e^{2t}$ and $x_2' = 3x_2$ gives $x_2 = c_2 e^{3t}$, the same general solution.

exercises.prompt: Find the general solution of $x_1' = 3 x_1 + x_2$, $x_2' = 2 x_1 + 4 x_2$ using the eigenvalue method.

answer.solution: Here $\kA = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ and $\det(\kA - \klambda\kI) = (3-\klambda)(4-\klambda) - 2 = \klambda^2 - 7\klambda + 10 = (\klambda-2)(\klambda-5)$. For $\klambda = 2$: $\kA - 2\kI = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, so $v_1 + v_2 = 0$ and $\kvecv = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. For $\klambda = 5$: $\kA - 5\kI = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, so $-2v_1 + v_2 = 0$ and $\kvecv = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. The general solution is $\kvecx = c_1\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]e^{2t} + c_2\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]e^{5t}$, that is $x_1 = c_1 e^{2t} + c_2 e^{5t}$ and $x_2 = -c_1 e^{2t} + 2c_2 e^{5t}$.

exercises.prompt: Find the general solution of $x_1' = x_1 -2 x_2$, $x_2' = 2 x_1 + x_2$ using the eigenvalue method. Do not use complex exponentials in your solution.

answer.solution: Here $\kP = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ and $\det(\kP - \klambda\kI) = (1-\klambda)^2 + 4 = \klambda^2 - 2\klambda + 5$, so $\klambda = 1 \pm 2i$. For $\klambda = 1+2i$: $\kP - (1+2i)\kI = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} -2i & -2 \\ 2 & -2i \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, whose first row gives $-2i v_1 - 2 v_2 = 0$; picking $v_2 = 1$ gives $\kvecv = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} i \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. By Euler’s formula $\kvecv e^{(1+2i)t} = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} i \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right] e^t(\cos 2t + i \sin 2t) = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} -e^t \sin 2t \\ e^t \cos 2t \end{smallmatrix} \right] + i\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} e^t \cos 2t \\ e^t \sin 2t \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. By Theorem 3.4.2 its real and imaginary parts are two linearly independent real-valued solutions, and the general solution is $\kvecx = c_1\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} -e^t \sin 2t \\ e^t \cos 2t \end{smallmatrix} \right] + c_2\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} e^t \cos 2t \\ e^t \sin 2t \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, that is $x_1 = -c_1 e^t \sin 2t + c_2 e^t \cos 2t$ and $x_2 = c_1 e^t \cos 2t + c_2 e^t \sin 2t$.

exercises.prompt:
1. Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $\kA = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 9 & -2 & -6 \\ -8 & 3 & 6 \\ 10 & -2 & -6 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$.
  2. Find the general solution of $\kvecxprime = \kA \kvecx$.

answer.solution: a) Expanding, $\det(\kA - \klambda\kI) = -\klambda^3 + 6\klambda^2 - 11\klambda + 6 = -(\klambda-1)(\klambda-2)(\klambda-3)$, so the eigenvalues are $1$, $2$, $3$. Solving $(\kA - \klambda\kI)\kvecv = \vec{0}$ for each: $\klambda = 1$ gives $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, $\klambda = 2$ gives $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \\ 3 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, and $\klambda = 3$ gives $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ 4 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ (or any nonzero multiples). For example $\kA\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ 4 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 27+6-24 \\ -24-9+24 \\ 30+6-24 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 9 \\ -9 \\ 12 \end{smallmatrix} \right] = 3\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ 4 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. b) The three eigenvalues are distinct and real, so by Theorem 3.4.1 $\kvecx = c_1\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]e^t + c_2\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \\ 3 \end{smallmatrix} \right]e^{2t} + c_3\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ 4 \end{smallmatrix} \right]e^{3t}$.

$\det(\kA - \klambda\kI) = -\klambda^3 + 3\klambda - 2 = -(\klambda-1)^2(\klambda+2)$, so the eigenvalues are $-2$ and $1$, the latter repeated. For $\klambda = -2$: $\kA + 2\kI = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ row reduces to $v_1 - v_3 = 0$, $v_2 + v_3 = 0$, and $v_3 = 1$ gives $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. For $\klambda = 1$: every row of $\kA - \kI = \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} -3 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \\ -3 & -1 & -1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ is a multiple of $[\, 3 \;\; 1 \;\; 1 \,]$, so the only equation is $3v_1 + v_2 + v_3 = 0$ with two free variables; two independent eigenvectors are $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ -3 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ and $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -3 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, and every nonzero combination of them is an eigenvector for $\klambda = 1$.

exercises.prompt: Let $a,b,c,d,e,f$ be numbers. Find the eigenvalues of $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} a & b & c \\ 0 & d & e \\ 0 & 0 & f \end{smallmatrix} \right]$.

answer.solution: Subtracting $\klambda\kI$ leaves $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} a-\klambda & b & c \\ 0 & d-\klambda & e \\ 0 & 0 & f-\klambda \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, still zero below the diagonal. Expanding the determinant along the first column, $\det = (a-\klambda)\bigl((d-\klambda)(f-\klambda) - e \cdot 0\bigr) = (a-\klambda)(d-\klambda)(f-\klambda)$, so $\det(\kA - \klambda\kI) = 0$ exactly when $\klambda = a$, $\klambda = d$ or $\klambda = f$: the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries $a$, $d$, $f$ (whatever $b$, $c$, $e$ are).

exercises.prompt:
1. Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $\kA= \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 & 3 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$.
  2. Solve the system $\kvecxprime = \kA \kvecx$.

answer.solution: a) Eigenvalues: $4,0,-1$ Eigenvectors: $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \\ -2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ b) $\kvecx = C_1 \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right] e^{4t} + C_2 \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right] + C_3 \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \\ -2 \end{smallmatrix} \right] e^{-t}$

exercises.prompt:
1. Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $\kA=\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$.
  2. Solve the system $\kvecxprime = \kA\kvecx$.

answer.solution: a) Eigenvalues: $\frac{1+\sqrt{3}i}{2}, \frac{1-\sqrt{3}i}{2}$, Eigenvectors: $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} -2 \\ 1-\sqrt{3}i \end{smallmatrix} \right]$, $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} -2 \\ 1+\sqrt{3}i \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ b) $\kvecx = C_1 e^{t/2} \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} -2\cos\bigl(\frac{\sqrt{3}t}{2}\bigr) \\ \cos\bigl(\frac{\sqrt{3}t}{2}\bigr) + \sqrt{3}\sin\bigl(\frac{\sqrt{3}t}{2}\bigr) \end{smallmatrix} \right] + C_2 e^{t/2} \left[ \begin{smallmatrix} - 2\sin\bigl(\frac{\sqrt{3}t}{2}\bigr) \\ \sin\bigl(\frac{\sqrt{3}t}{2}\bigr) -\sqrt{3}\cos\bigl(\frac{\sqrt{3}t}{2}\bigr) \end{smallmatrix} \right]$

exercises.prompt: Solve $x_1' = x_2$, $x_2' = x_1$ using the eigenvalue method.
